title: Tsunami siren on the beach
advice: Do not drive: roads out of coastal towns jam fast (Japan 2011 survey: about a third of evacuees got stuck in traffic)
If the sea suddenly pulls back far from the shore, a wave is coming - move immediately
Go up if you cannot go far: a strong reinforced concrete or steel building, above the 4th floor
The first wave is often not the biggest; waves can keep coming for hours - stay up until officials say it is safe
sources: NOAA/NWS tsunami safety; Honolulu vertical evacuation policy; Japan Cabinet Office 2011 evacuation survey
moves: walk_to_shelter, then climb_shelter (the hotel roof); the wave hits only after the hero is up

title: Lost in a forest as night falls
advice: Stop as soon as you realize you are lost - most people make it worse by walking further (S.T.O.P.: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan)
Stay put near where you are: searchers start from your last known point
Make yourself visible and audible: bright clothing in the open, three whistle blasts is a distress signal
Before dark, get out of the wind and off the cold ground: branches or leaves under you, shelter close to a tree or rock
sources: US National Park Service, US Forest Service hiking safety; Hug-a-Tree program
moves: the hero stays put near the trees (crouch / wave to be seen); do NOT walk to the cabin far away - staying put is the advice

title: City-wide blackout for days
advice: Keep the fridge and freezer closed: a closed fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours
Never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors or in a garage - carbon monoxide kills silently
Store water early: fill containers and the bathtub while taps still work
Use flashlights, not candles - candles cause house fires during blackouts
sources: Ready.gov power outages; USDA food safety; CDC carbon monoxide
moves: lights go out first (use fx lights_off), then the hero walks_to_shelter (home building) and enter_shelter

title: Stuck in your car in a blizzard
advice: Stay with the car - it is shelter and easier for rescuers to find than a person in the snow
Run the engine about 10 minutes each hour for heat, with a window cracked a little
Clear snow from the exhaust pipe first - a blocked pipe fills the car with carbon monoxide
Tie a bright cloth to the antenna or door; turn on the inside light at night so crews can see you
sources: Ready.gov winter storms; National Weather Service winter safety
moves: the hero starts inside the car (heroStart inside); snow builds up; the hero stays with the car

title: Falling through the ice
advice: The first minute is cold shock: do not panic, control your breathing (the 1-10-1 rule: 1 minute to breathe, about 10 minutes of useful movement, about 1 hour before you pass out from cold)
Turn back toward the direction you came from - that ice held your weight
Put your arms flat on the ice, kick your legs to get your body horizontal, and pull yourself out
Do not stand up - roll away from the hole to spread your weight, then crawl to shore
sources: Minnesota DNR ice safety; Cold Water Boot Camp (1-10-1 rule)
moves: the ice cracks under the hero first; then the hero crouches (rolls), then walk_to_shelter = the shore

title: Earthquake hits while you are at home
advice: Drop, Cover, Hold On: drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table, hold on
Do not run outside during shaking - most injuries come from falling objects and debris near buildings
Stay away from windows, glass and tall furniture
After shaking stops, expect aftershocks; check for gas smell and leave if you smell it
moves: the hero starts inside the house; shaking first; then crouch (drop, cover, hold on); do NOT run outside

title: Wildfire blocks the road out
advice: Leave early when told to evacuate - waiting is the most dangerous choice
If trapped in a car: park in an area clear of vegetation, close windows and vents, keep the engine running
Get down on the floor and cover yourself with a wool blanket or jacket; the car is safer than running on foot
If on foot, head for ground with little fuel: a road, a rocky area, or already burned ground
sources: Ready.gov wildfires; NFPA; CAL FIRE Ready Set Go
moves: the hero runs away from the fire to bare ground (run_away), then crouch; do NOT enter the wooden cabin

title: Tornado warning at home
advice: Go to the basement, or an interior room on the lowest floor with no windows
Put as many walls as possible between you and the outside
Cover your head and neck with your arms, a mattress or helmets
Mobile homes and cars are not safe - get to a sturdy building
sources: National Weather Service tornado safety; Ready.gov
moves: the hero enters the house and goes to the basement (enter_shelter), then crouch

title: Car breaks down in the desert
advice: Stay with the car: a vehicle is much easier to spot than a person
Rest in the shade during the hottest hours; move, if you must, early morning or evening
Drink the water you have when thirsty - rationing water while you overheat does not help
Signal: raise the hood, use a mirror to flash sunlight, keep your phone for when you get signal
sources: US National Park Service desert safety (Death Valley); Ready.gov extreme heat
moves: the hero walks to the rock shade (walk_to_shelter), stays near it, waves to signal

title: Caught in an avalanche
advice: Try to get off the slab to the side as it starts
If you are swept away, fight to stay on the surface - swimming motions, dump your heavy pack if you can
As the snow slows, push one hand up toward the surface and cup your other arm in front of your face for an air pocket
Rescue gear matters: a beacon, probe and shovel - most buried people need to be dug out within about 15 minutes
sources: Avalanche.org (US avalanche centers); Utah Avalanche Center
moves: the snow hits first; the hero crouches (air pocket), then waves a hand

title: Fire alarm wakes you at night
advice: Get low and go: smoke rises, the cleanest air is near the floor
Feel the door with the back of your hand before opening; if it is hot, use another way out
Close doors behind you to slow the fire
Get out, stay out, call for help from outside - never go back in
sources: NFPA; American Red Cross home fire safety
moves: the hero starts inside the house (heroStart inside), crouches low (smoke), then run_away out of the house; never goes back

title: Flash flood on the road
advice: Turn Around, Don't Drown: never drive into flooded roads
About 12 inches (30 cm) of moving water can carry away most cars, and 6 inches can knock an adult off their feet
If water surrounds the car and is rising, get out and move to higher ground if you safely can
Flood water hides holes, washed-out roads and debris
moves: the hero leaves the car and run_away to higher ground before the water rises

title: Thunderstorm above the tree line
advice: When thunder roars, go indoors - no place outside is truly safe; a building or hard-top car is
Get off peaks and ridges right away and head down
Never shelter under a lone tree or near metal fences
Spread a group out so one strike does not hit everyone
moves: the storm starts first; the hero run_away down the mountain, avoids lone trees, then enter_shelter (rock)

title: Hurricane storm surge
advice: If officials say evacuate, go - water (storm surge and flooding), not wind, causes most hurricane deaths
Run from the water, hide from the wind: leave surge zones, then shelter in a sturdy building
Stay away from windows, in an interior room
Do not walk or drive through flood water after the storm; watch for downed power lines
moves: the hero walk_to_shelter then enter_shelter (sturdy building interior) before the surge hits
